title: Project Management Professional (PMP)

exam.scoring: Pass/fail determined against PMI proficiency thresholds across all three domains

content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the PMI PMP Exam Content Outline (the three official domains and their weightings). Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.stem: During a sprint, two senior developers disagree strongly about the system architecture, and the debate is delaying progress. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Facilitate a session so both developers can present their views and agree on a path forward
Escalate the disagreement to the project sponsor for a decision
Direct the more senior developer to make the call and move on
Reassign one of the developers to another team to end the conflict
items.explanation: PMI favours resolving conflict directly through collaborative problem-solving before any escalation. Escalating or imposing a decision removes ownership and leaves the root cause, while reassigning a person avoids rather than resolves the disagreement.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: Two project managers both need the same database specialist at the same time, and neither project can proceed without them. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Ask the specialist to work overtime for both projects
Meet with the other project manager to negotiate a shared schedule based on project priorities
Escalate to the PMO to force a decision
Proceed without the specialist and catch up later
items.explanation: Negotiating directly with the peer is the collaborative first step and keeps ownership with the project managers. Escalation is a last resort, working without a key resource creates schedule risk, and sustained overtime is not a sustainable solution.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Resource Management

items.stem: A team member reports that a colleague's behaviour is undermining morale but asks the project manager to keep the conversation private. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Document the complaint and forward it to human resources immediately
Ignore it because it is a personal matter between team members
Meet the individuals privately to understand the situation and address the behaviour
Call a full team meeting to discuss morale openly
items.explanation: The project manager should honour the confidence, gather facts privately, and address the behaviour directly. A public meeting breaks trust, immediate escalation is premature before understanding, and ignoring it lets morale and performance deteriorate.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: On a distributed team, a misunderstanding between members from different cultures has caused tension. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Reorganize the team so those members no longer work together
Send a written reminder that all communication must be in one language
Report the incident to the sponsor as a resource risk
Facilitate a conversation that builds shared understanding of each member's communication style
items.explanation: Building shared understanding is core to a People domain task and leverages diversity rather than suppressing it. Reorganizing avoids the issue, a language mandate does not address working norms, and escalating before any attempt to resolve is premature.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: Two team members argue because one wants to work remotely full time while the other expects everyone on site. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Review the team charter and ground rules with the team and agree on working arrangements
Order both members to return to the office full time
Let each member work however they prefer
Escalate the scheduling dispute to the sponsor
items.explanation: Agreed ground rules and the team charter are the reference point for working norms. A unilateral order ignores team agreements, a laissez-faire approach creates inequity, and escalation bypasses a matter the team can settle.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: The team believes a requirement is technically infeasible, but the stakeholder insists it is mandatory. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Escalate to the sponsor to decide
Bring the team and stakeholder together to clarify the requirement and explore alternatives
Tell the team to implement the requirement exactly as directed
Remove the requirement from scope to avoid delay
items.explanation: Collaborating to clarify needs and generate options respects both the stakeholder and the team. Forcing an infeasible requirement harms quality, unilaterally cutting scope is a change without authority, and escalation before attempting resolution is premature.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A project manager is assigned to lead an existing team that has low trust in management. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Announce new performance targets to raise accountability
Request a new team because this one is dysfunctional
Meet the team to listen to their concerns and understand their history
Replace the lowest performers to reset the team
items.explanation: Trust is rebuilt by listening and understanding first. Replacing members or resetting targets before diagnosis erodes trust further and signals the same management pattern, while requesting a new team avoids the leadership task entirely.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: In an agile project the team seems unsure why their work matters. What should the project manager do?
options: Add more detailed task assignments for each member
Increase the number of daily stand-ups
Ask the sponsor to visit the team every week
Clarify and communicate the product vision and how the team's work delivers value
items.explanation: As a servant leader the project manager keeps purpose and value visible. More task assignments are micromanagement, additional ceremonies add overhead without meaning, and sponsor visits cannot replace a clearly articulated vision.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: A junior team member is eager but has limited experience with a key task. Which leadership approach is BEST?
options: Provide direct guidance and close support while the member builds competence
Delegate the task fully and check in only at the deadline
Assign another team member to perform the task instead
Use a laissez-faire approach so the member learns by failing
items.explanation: Situational leadership matches a directive-coaching style to low competence and high commitment. Full delegation risks failure, taking the task away prevents growth, and a laissez-faire style is inappropriate for a novice on key work.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: The team missed a critical milestone and morale is low. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Add overtime across the team to recover the schedule
Hold a blameless review to identify causes and refocus the team on next steps
Post a schedule of penalties for future misses
Escalate the miss to the sponsor immediately
items.explanation: A blameless, problem-solving review addresses causes and rebuilds momentum. Penalties damage morale, escalation before analysis adds no diagnosis, and blanket overtime is neither first nor necessarily sustainable.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A global team spans many time zones and collaboration is suffering. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Disband the distributed team and co-locate the members
Reduce communication to a weekly status email
Agree with the team on communication norms and meeting times that balance time zones
Require everyone to be online during the headquarters workday
items.explanation: Co-creating norms and rotating meeting times respects the distributed team and improves engagement. A headquarters-centric schedule disadvantages most members, co-location is often infeasible, and cutting communication worsens the problem.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A team member asks the project manager to approve a report the project manager knows contains inaccurate estimates. What should the project manager do?
options: Approve it to avoid conflict and fix it later
Submit the report and blame the team member if it is questioned
Ask a colleague to sign off on it instead
Decline the approval and correct the estimates with the team before submitting
items.explanation: The PMI Code of Ethics requires honesty and accuracy, so the project manager must not sanction false data. Approving it or shifting blame is unethical, and asking someone else to sign evades rather than resolves the responsibility.
items.reference: PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct

items.stem: A decision will affect how the team works day to day. What approach BEST supports commitment to the decision?
options: Involve the affected team members in making the decision
Make the decision alone and inform the team afterward
Delay the decision until the sponsor weighs in
Let the most senior member decide for everyone
items.explanation: Participatory decision-making on matters that affect the team builds ownership and commitment. Deciding unilaterally or delegating to seniority reduces buy-in, and deferring to the sponsor for a team-level matter is unnecessary.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: The team delivered a difficult release ahead of schedule. What should the project manager do?
options: Say nothing in order to avoid appearing to favour the team
Acknowledge the team's achievement and share the recognition with stakeholders
Immediately assign the next backlog items to keep momentum
Take personal credit to strengthen the project's standing
items.explanation: Timely recognition reinforces motivation and team performance. Moving straight to more work ignores effort, claiming credit is unethical, and staying silent misses a low-cost opportunity to strengthen engagement.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A newly formed team is unclear about how it will operate. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Wait for problems to appear and then set rules
Ask the PMO to issue standard team rules
Facilitate creation of a team charter covering norms, roles, and decision rules
Write detailed procedures and distribute them to the team
items.explanation: A team charter co-created by the team establishes working agreements and ownership. Top-down procedures or PMO rules reduce ownership, and waiting for problems invites avoidable conflict and rework.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: During a retrospective the team admits that members keep interrupting one another in meetings. What should the project manager do?
options: Warn the team that meetings will be cancelled if interruptions continue
Allow the behaviour because open debate is valuable
Move all discussions to a written format
Work with the team to update the ground rules and model respectful discussion
items.explanation: Updating ground rules together and modelling the behaviour is the constructive response. Threats are punitive, tolerating interruptions harms inclusion, and moving everything to writing limits the collaboration the team needs.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A team member consistently misses commitments, slowing the whole team. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Meet privately to understand the cause and agree on a support plan
Publicly reassign the member's tasks to others
Document the misses and begin the termination process
Escalate directly to the functional manager
items.explanation: The first step is to understand the cause and offer support, which may resolve the performance gap. Public reassignment humiliates the member, termination is premature, and escalating before coaching skips the project manager's responsibility.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: The project manager wants to set clear performance expectations for the team. What is the BEST approach?
options: Wait until the first formal performance review to set expectations
Agree on measurable goals and responsibilities with each team member
Impose quotas without discussion
Rely on the team to define their own goals with no review
items.explanation: Collaboratively agreed, measurable goals give clarity and ownership. Imposed quotas reduce commitment, unreviewed self-set goals may not align with the project, and waiting until a formal review leaves the team without direction.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: The project manager needs to know whether the team is on track toward its goals. Which action is BEST?
options: Ask the sponsor to assess the team's performance
Assume progress because no one has raised an issue
Review agreed performance metrics and delivery progress with the team regularly
Check progress only at phase gates
items.explanation: Regular review of agreed metrics against goals is how team performance is supported and corrective action triggered early. Phase-gate-only checks are too infrequent, the sponsor is not the team's assessor, and assuming progress ignores emerging problems.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A team member's work quality has improved recently, but they rarely receive feedback. What should the project manager do?
options: Save all feedback until the annual review
Only give feedback when mistakes occur
Let peers deliver all feedback to the member
Give timely, specific positive and constructive feedback
items.explanation: Frequent, specific feedback sustains improvement and engagement. Delaying feedback removes its value, feedback only on errors is demotivating, and delegating all feedback to peers fails the leader's responsibility.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: The team has worked long hours for several weeks and is showing signs of burnout. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Discuss workload and sustainability with the team and rebalance the work
Offer bonuses to encourage continued overtime
Replace the most fatigued team members
Ignore it until the next milestone is reached
items.explanation: Sustainable pace protects quality and retention, so the project manager should address workload with the team. Bonuses do not fix systemic overload, replacing people is disruptive and unfair, and ignoring burnout risks attrition and defects.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: An agile team is repeatedly blocked by a slow approval process outside their control. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Ask the team to estimate around the delay
Identify the blocker and work to remove or escalate it so the team can proceed
Tell the team to work around the approval step
Add the blocker to the next sprint review agenda
items.explanation: Removing impediments is a core servant-leadership duty. Working around a required control may breach governance, merely adding an agenda item does not unblock the team, and estimating around a delay does not remove it.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: The team lacks a skill needed for an upcoming feature. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Ask the team to learn the skill on their own time
Reduce scope to avoid needing the skill
Assess the gap and arrange training or coaching for the team
Outsource the entire feature immediately
items.explanation: Ensuring team members are adequately trained is a People domain task; assess the gap and close it. Outsourcing or cutting scope may be options later, and expecting unpaid self-study signals poor support for the team.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: Stakeholders will need to use a new system after go-live but have not been trained. What should the project manager do?
options: Provide a written manual only and assume it is sufficient
Delay training until problems appear after go-live
Ask the vendor to handle all training without involving the project
Plan and deliver training so stakeholders can use the deliverable effectively
items.explanation: Adequate training enables adoption and benefits realization, so it must be planned before go-live. A manual alone is often insufficient, waiting for problems creates avoidable disruption, and fully delegating training loses project context.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A new project coordinator wants to grow into a project manager role. What should the project manager do?
options: Mentor them by sharing experience and giving stretch opportunities
Assign them only administrative tasks
Advise them to wait until they have more seniority
Tell them to apply toward a project manager role in another department
items.explanation: Mentoring and stretch assignments develop people and are a People domain responsibility. Limiting work to administration or telling them to wait or leave fails to support growth and may lose a motivated contributor.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A project manager notices that they become irritable when under deadline pressure. What should they do?
options: Ask the team to stop raising issues near deadlines
Recognize the emotion, manage the reaction, and model calm behaviour
Avoid the team whenever they feel stressed
Blame the schedule for the tension in front of the team
items.explanation: Emotional intelligence begins with self-awareness and self-management, so the leader should regulate their own reaction and model composure. Avoiding the team, blaming the schedule, or suppressing input all damage trust and performance.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: The organization announces layoffs that will affect the project team. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Focus only on keeping the schedule on track
Tell the team their jobs are safe in order to calm them
Acknowledge the team's emotions and communicate what is known with empathy
Say nothing until the formal announcement is made
items.explanation: Leading with empathy and honest, timely information supports the team through uncertainty. Silence breeds rumour, ignoring emotions erodes trust, and making false assurances is unethical and harmful.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: In a tense meeting a stakeholder makes a personal attack on the project manager. What is the BEST response?
options: Respond in kind to defend their reputation
Walk out of the meeting
Threaten to escalate the stakeholder's behaviour to the sponsor
Stay composed, acknowledge the concern, and redirect the discussion to the issue
items.explanation: Self-regulation and focus on the problem, not the person, de-escalates and keeps the project moving. Retaliating, leaving, or threatening escalation all inflame the situation and model poor emotional intelligence.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: A stakeholder is visibly frustrated about repeated delays. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Listen to the stakeholder's concerns and acknowledge their impact
Explain that the delays are the team's fault
Send a detailed schedule to distract them from the delay
Ask the sponsor to handle the stakeholder instead
items.explanation: Empathetic listening first lowers tension and builds a basis for problem-solving. Blaming the team damages trust, using data to distract avoids the concern, and passing the stakeholder to the sponsor abdicates the relationship.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A new team is hesitant to raise risks openly. What should the project manager do to build trust?
options: Wait for trust to develop on its own
Create a safe environment where concerns can be raised without blame
Require risks to be reported in writing with the reporter's name
Reward the members who report the most risks
items.explanation: Psychological safety is built when people can speak up without fear of blame. Mandatory named reporting increases fear, rewarding risk counts games the metric, and passively waiting fails to lead the culture.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: A team member privately admits a mistake that could affect the deliverable. What should the project manager do?
options: Warn them that mistakes will affect their performance review
Quietly fix it and keep it from stakeholders
Thank them, focus on solving the issue, and avoid punishing honesty
Publicly document the mistake as a lesson for the team
items.explanation: Rewarding candour and solving the problem reinforces psychological safety. Public exposure and threats discourage future disclosure, while hiding the issue from stakeholders is dishonest and may compound the impact.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: The project manager suspects the team is agreeing too quickly without exploring alternatives. What should they do?
options: Accept the consensus to save time
Make the decision alone to break the cycle
Bring in an external consultant to challenge the team
Encourage dissenting views and actively invite quieter members to contribute
items.explanation: Guarding against groupthink means deliberately seeking divergent input and including quieter voices. Accepting premature consensus risks poor decisions, deciding alone removes ownership, and hiring a consultant is disproportionate.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: A hybrid team struggles to keep information consistent across multiple sites. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Establish shared collaboration tools and a single source of truth
Require all decisions to be made at headquarters
Rely on word of mouth between sites
Hold a single weekly call to transmit all information
items.explanation: Shared tools and one source of truth give a distributed team consistent information. Headquarters-only decisions disenfranchise sites, word of mouth is unreliable, and a single weekly call is too limited a channel strategy.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: Remote team members report feeling disconnected from the project. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Replace remote members with co-located staff
Increase purposeful engagement through inclusive virtual meetings and regular check-ins
Require remote members to travel monthly
Assign them more independent work to reduce the need to interact
items.explanation: Intentional engagement keeps virtual team members included and motivated. Mandatory travel is costly and may be infeasible, isolating remote members deepens disconnection, and replacing them discards talent.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A team that has just formed will need to work closely together for a year. What should the project manager do?
options: Focus only on technical tasks and expect relationships to form
Wait until conflicts appear before addressing relationships
Invest in team-building and relationship activities early
Skip team-building to save time and cost
items.explanation: Early team-building helps a forming team move through storming into effective performance. Skipping it or waiting for conflict to emerge predictably slows the team, and relationships rarely improve on their own under pressure.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: A functional manager can only spare a specialist on a part-time basis. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Demand the specialist full time through the sponsor
Use whoever is available regardless of skill
Delay the work until the specialist becomes fully free
Negotiate the specialist's availability and priorities with the functional manager
items.explanation: Negotiating is the resource-conflict response that best respects the functional manager's constraints. Demanding through the sponsor damages the relationship, using unskilled staff harms quality, and indefinite delay ignores the schedule.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Resource Management

items.stem: A vendor team will deliver part of the solution. What should the project manager do to set expectations?
options: Negotiate a clear agreement covering deliverables, quality, and communication
Assume the contract already covers every expectation
Let the vendor choose their own standards independently
Communicate with the vendor only at the end of delivery
items.explanation: Negotiating an agreement on deliverables, quality, and communication prevents mismatched expectations. Assuming the contract covers all conduct is risky, letting the vendor set standards may break requirements, and end-only communication invites surprises.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: Team members and stakeholders use different terms for the same requirement. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Document the terms privately and never discuss them
Establish a shared glossary and confirm common understanding
Correct people whenever they use the wrong term
Ignore it because experts understand one another
items.explanation: A shared glossary builds the common understanding that prevents rework and miscommunication. Publicly correcting people damages relationships, assuming mutual understanding is unjustified, and private notes do not align the group.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A virtual team keeps missing important updates. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Call each member individually every day
Ask the sponsor to relay updates to the team
Agree on a communication plan covering channels, cadence, and escalation
Send more frequent emails to everyone
items.explanation: A deliberate communication plan matches message to channel and cadence for a virtual team. More email may add noise, daily calls are inefficient, and using the sponsor as a relay is inappropriate and slow.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: Some team members arrive late to stand-ups and it unsettles the others. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Cancel the stand-ups
Publicly name and shame the individuals who arrive late
Accept it because stand-ups are informal
Remind the team of the agreed ground rules and address the pattern
items.explanation: Consistently applying the team's ground rules reinforces shared expectations. Cancelling stand-ups removes a valuable cadence, shaming individuals is destructive, and tolerating lateness erodes the team norms.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: A new member joins the team mid-project. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Provide onboarding on the project's goals, standards, and how the team works
Let them observe silently for a month before contributing
Assign the hardest task immediately to test their ability
Give them only the technical documentation to read
items.explanation: Proper onboarding accelerates contribution and reduces risk of mistakes. Silent observation wastes weeks, immediately testing with hard work sets them up to fail, and documentation alone omits context and relationships.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: Critical knowledge is held by a single team member. What should the project manager do to reduce risk?
options: Keep the knowledge confidential to protect the project's value
Promote knowledge sharing such as pairing, reviews, and documentation
Ask the member to work more hours
Accept the single point of knowledge as normal
items.explanation: Spreading knowledge through pairing, reviews, and documentation reduces key-person risk. Adding hours does not reduce dependency, accepting it leaves a serious exposure, and hoarding knowledge increases fragility.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: A complex module must be understood by more than one developer. What should the project manager do?
options: Document it once and file the documentation
Delay the module until more staff are hired
Arrange pair programming or code reviews to spread understanding
Assign it to the strongest developer to work alone
items.explanation: Pairing and reviews deliberately share understanding of complex work. Solo ownership concentrates risk, a single document may be inaccurate or ignored, and delaying for hiring is disproportionate when a simple practice solves the problem.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: The team has single points of failure in two critical roles. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Hire backups for both roles
Accept the risk as unavoidable
Document the risk and take no action
Cross-train members so work can continue if someone is unavailable
items.explanation: Cross-training is a practical, low-cost way to remove single points of failure. Hiring backups may be slow and costly, and merely accepting or documenting the risk without action leaves the project exposed.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A key architect plans to leave in three months. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Plan knowledge transfer and identify a successor
Ask the architect to stay longer without any transition plan
Recruit a replacement only after the architect leaves
Reduce project scope to eliminate the architect's work
items.explanation: Forward planning for knowledge transfer and succession protects continuity. Asking them to stay without a plan is not a safeguard, waiting to recruit creates a capability gap, and cutting scope to avoid the issue is disproportionate.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: The team asks the project manager to make every routine decision. What should the project manager do?
options: Escalate routine decisions to the sponsor
Empower the team to decide within agreed boundaries and support them
Continue deciding everything to retain control
Refuse to help with any decision
items.explanation: Empowerment within clear boundaries builds capability and capacity. Retaining every decision creates a bottleneck, refusing all help is unhelpful, and escalating routine matters wastes governance time.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: The project manager is overloaded with tasks the team could handle. What should they do?
options: Delegate only the most trivial tasks
Ask the sponsor to approve additional staff
Delegate appropriate work with clear authority and support
Keep all tasks so they stay fully informed
items.explanation: Delegating meaningful work with authority develops the team and relieves the bottleneck. Hoarding tasks harms flow, delegating only trivia does not address the overload, and requesting more staff may be unnecessary and slow.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: An agile team keeps waiting for the project manager to assign tasks. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue assigning tasks to keep things moving
Add a layer of team leads to distribute the work
Change the team back to a traditional managed model
Coach the team to self-organize and pull work as a team
items.explanation: Self-organization is central to agile, so the leader should coach the behaviour rather than sustain dependency. Assigning tasks or adding leads entrenches command-and-control, and reverting to traditional management abandons agile benefits.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: A sponsor asks for daily detailed reports on each team member's activity. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Discuss reporting needs with the sponsor and agree on meaningful, lighter indicators
Produce the daily detailed reports exactly as requested
Refuse to provide any reporting at all
Ask the team to write their own daily personal reports
items.explanation: The project manager should negotiate reporting that informs without micromanaging. Complying with detailed daily surveillance harms the team, refusing all reporting breaks accountability, and pushing reports onto the team burdens them further.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: The team is blocked waiting for a decision from another department. What should the project manager do?
options: Wait for the department to respond in their own time
Actively pursue the decision and remove the blocker for the team
Tell the team to proceed on assumptions
Report the blocker in the monthly status report
items.explanation: A servant leader removes impediments promptly. Proceeding on assumptions may cause rework, merely reporting the blocker leaves the team stuck, and passive waiting lets schedule risk grow.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A team member asks the project manager to solve a problem they could handle with some guidance. What is the BEST response?
options: Tell them it is not the project manager's responsibility
Escalate it to their functional manager
Coach them through the options so they can solve it themselves
Solve it for them to save time
items.explanation: Coaching builds capability and future independence. Solving it for them creates dependency, refusing to help is dismissive, and escalating a coaching opportunity to the functional manager wastes their time.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: The team is stuck debating two technical options and cannot decide. What should the project manager do?
options: Choose the option the project manager personally prefers
Postpone the decision indefinitely
Let the debate continue without any structure
Facilitate a decision by helping the team weigh criteria and reach agreement
items.explanation: Facilitation helps the team make an informed, owned decision. Imposing a personal preference removes ownership, indefinite postponement delays the project, and unstructured debate wastes time.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: Two stakeholders want conflicting changes to the same feature. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Facilitate a discussion to align on priorities and the impact of each option
Implement both changes to satisfy everyone
Escalate to the sponsor immediately
Choose the change requested by the more senior stakeholder
items.explanation: Facilitating a priorities-and-impact discussion resolves the conflict at the right level. Implementing both may exceed budget and confuse the design, immediate escalation skips a resolvable step, and deferring to seniority ignores merit.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A key stakeholder resists a change the project must deliver. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Exclude the stakeholder from further communications
Engage the stakeholder early to understand their concerns and build support
Proceed and ignore the resistance
Escalate the resistance to the sponsor
items.explanation: Early engagement to understand concerns is how resistance is reduced. Ignoring it builds an adversary, escalation before engagement is premature, and excluding a key stakeholder guarantees obstruction.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: The team must adopt a new way of working but members disagree about it. What should the project manager do?
options: Defer the decision to the PMO
Let each member work however they prefer
Facilitate consensus by aligning on shared goals and addressing concerns
Impose the new way by authority
items.explanation: Building consensus around shared goals gains commitment to the change. Imposing it invites passive resistance, deferring to the PMO avoids leadership, and letting everyone work differently prevents the intended improvement.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: A stakeholder doubts that the project will succeed. What should the project manager do?
options: Avoid them until results speak for themselves
Accept their opposition as permanently fixed
Report their negative attitude to the sponsor
Engage them early, share progress, and address concerns transparently
items.explanation: Transparent, early engagement can turn a skeptic into a supporter. Avoidance lets doubt grow, treating opposition as fixed gives up on the relationship, and reporting them as a problem is adversarial.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A stakeholder assumes a feature will be delivered sooner than the schedule shows. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Clarify the realistic schedule and reconcile expectations with the stakeholder
Promise the earlier date to keep the stakeholder happy
Say nothing and deliver on the later date
Add resources to meet the assumed date without analysis
items.explanation: Managing expectations means correcting the assumption with evidence. Promising an unrealistic date damages credibility, silence leads to a breach of expectation, and adding resources without analysis may not be feasible.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A dispute between two departments is beyond the project manager's authority and is blocking the project. What should the project manager do?
options: Pause the project without telling anyone
Escalate to the appropriate governance level with the facts and impact
Keep trying to resolve it indefinitely without authority
Make a decision that exceeds their authority
items.explanation: Escalation is appropriate when a matter exceeds the project manager's authority and blocks progress. Endless attempts waste time, overstepping authority sets a bad precedent, and silently pausing the project is unacceptable.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: Two team members need a solution that satisfies both of their requirements. Which conflict approach is BEST for the long term?
options: Force one member's preferred solution
Withdraw and let them resolve it later
Collaborate to find a solution that fully addresses both sets of needs
Compromise so each member gives up something
items.explanation: Collaboration produces a durable, win-win outcome and is preferred when time allows. Compromise leaves both partly unsatisfied, forcing creates a loser, and withdrawal avoids rather than resolves the conflict.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: A production outage requires an immediate decision and time is critical. Which conflict approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Hold a lengthy consensus workshop before acting
Withdraw and let the team decide once they are ready
Compromise on a partial fix regardless of impact
Make a decisive call now and revisit it in a blameless review later
items.explanation: In an emergency the forcing approach is appropriate because speed matters; the decision can be reviewed afterward. A lengthy workshop, withdrawal, or an indiscriminate partial fix all risk prolonging the outage.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: Two teams need to share a limited test environment so both can make progress. Which approach is BEST?
options: Negotiate a compromise that gives each team essential access time
Let the first team keep exclusive access
Escalate the environment contention to the sponsor
Avoid the decision until the environment frees up
items.explanation: A negotiated compromise lets both teams progress when resources are genuinely limited. Exclusive access starves the other team, escalation is avoidable here, and avoiding the decision stalls both teams.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: A minor disagreement arises over meeting logistics. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Document it as a formal issue in the issue log
Acknowledge it and let the team settle it without escalation
Escalate to the sponsor immediately
Force a decision to prevent any discussion
items.explanation: Trivial matters are best delegated to the team, which builds autonomy. Escalating or formalising a minor logistics question wastes governance capacity, and forcing a decision needlessly suppresses the team.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A reorganization has left the team uncertain about their future. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Focus only on tasks and ignore the uncertainty
Promise the team that no changes will occur
Communicate openly about what the change means for the project and the team
Say nothing until all decisions are final
items.explanation: Honest, timely communication reduces uncertainty and rumour. Silence lets anxiety grow, ignoring it harms engagement, and promising no change may be a false assurance.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A long project has few visible results and stakeholder interest is fading. What should the project manager do?
options: Wait until the final delivery to update stakeholders
Add more milestones without deliverables
Reduce stakeholder communication to save effort
Deliver and publicize incremental wins to sustain engagement
items.explanation: Incremental value and regular communication keep stakeholders invested. Waiting for the end risks disengagement, empty milestones are not real progress, and reducing communication worsens the problem.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A serious issue threatens the project and rumours are spreading. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Communicate promptly and honestly with the team and stakeholders
Withhold all information until the issue is fully resolved
Let the sponsor communicate everything to the team
Deny the issue to prevent panic
items.explanation: Prompt, honest communication counters rumour and maintains trust. Withholding information fuels speculation, relying solely on the sponsor is slow, and denying a real issue is unethical and damaging.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: The team has heard unfounded rumours that the project will be cancelled. What should the project manager do?
options: Confirm the cancellation to reduce the team's uncertainty
Share accurate, timely information to counter the misinformation
Ignore the rumours because they are harmless
Warn the team not to spread rumours
items.explanation: Accurate, timely information is the antidote to rumour. Ignoring it lets fear spread, simply telling people to stop talking does not address the cause, and confirming a falsehood is harmful and dishonest.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: An agile team's velocity has dropped for three consecutive sprints. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Report the team as underperforming to management
Lengthen the sprint without any analysis
Work with the team to identify and address the causes of the drop
Push the team to work harder and raise velocity
items.explanation: Velocity is a diagnostic signal, so the project manager should investigate root causes with the team. Pushing harder ignores the cause, reporting the team erodes trust, and changing sprint length without analysis treats a symptom.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: Retrospectives keep generating improvement ideas that are never implemented. What should the project manager do?
options: Stop holding retrospectives since they waste time
Limit each retrospective to a single idea
Assign all improvement actions to the project manager
Ensure action items are owned, tracked, and followed up between retrospectives
items.explanation: The value of a retrospective comes from acting on its output, so improvements need owners and follow-up. Cancelling or limiting the session wastes the practice, and centralising every action on the leader is unsustainable.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: A team member regularly bypasses agreed processes, causing rework. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Discuss the behaviour privately and reinforce the agreed ground rules
Escalate to the functional manager immediately
Ignore it to avoid conflict
Let the team manage it with no guidance
items.explanation: A private, direct conversation reinforces norms and preserves dignity. Immediate escalation skips the project manager's responsibility, ignoring it condones rework, and leaving it entirely to the team may leave it unaddressed.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: The team agreed to timebox meetings, but one member consistently overruns. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask other members to leave when time is up
Remind the team of the ground rule and apply it consistently
Cancel the meetings altogether
Allow the overruns to avoid confrontation
items.explanation: Ground rules work only when applied consistently, so the leader should reinforce them. Cancelling loses the cadence, allowing overruns invalidates the agreement, and leaving mid-meeting is disruptive and passive-aggressive.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: A project manager feels a strong urge to react angrily after a setback. What is the BEST action?
options: Suppress the emotion and say nothing at all
Blame the team to release the pressure
Pause, manage the reaction, and respond thoughtfully
Express the anger openly to show they care about the project
items.explanation: Self-management means pausing and choosing a constructive response. Venting anger damages trust, total suppression fails to address the issue, and blaming the team is unfair and destructive.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: A team member is describing a problem, but the project manager keeps jumping to solutions. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue offering quick solutions to save time
Interrupt to keep the conversation short
Ask someone else to listen on the project manager's behalf
Listen fully and confirm understanding before offering solutions
items.explanation: Active listening means hearing the whole problem and confirming understanding before solving. Jumping in or interrupting misses information, and delegating listening weakens the relationship.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: A team member's idea resolved a major obstacle. What should the project manager do?
options: Give public credit to the team member
Present the idea as the project manager's own
Mention the team generally without naming anyone
Say nothing in order to avoid jealousy
items.explanation: Public recognition of the individual reinforces motivation and reinforces ethical leadership. Claiming credit is dishonest, vague credit weakens the gesture, and silence misses a chance to reinforce the behaviour.
items.reference: PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct

items.stem: A valued team member is distracted by a personal crisis and their work is slipping. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Ignore it until the next performance review
Speak privately with empathy and agree on temporary support
Immediately reassign all their critical work
Formally discipline them for the drop in output
items.explanation: Empathetic, private conversation with practical support is the human and effective first step. Reassigning or disciplining before understanding is harsh and premature, and ignoring it lets performance decline.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A remote team member seems disengaged and rarely speaks in meetings. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Replace them with a co-located team member
Call them out in front of the whole team
Reach out one-on-one to understand their experience and involve them
Assume they are content because they have not complained
items.explanation: A private check-in uncovers the cause and shows care. Assuming all is well misses a warning sign, replacing them is drastic, and public confrontation would deepen disengagement.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - People domain

items.stem: A team comes from many backgrounds and the project manager wants everyone to contribute. What should the project manager do?
options: Standardize everyone's approach to a single preferred style
Prefer contributors who match the majority culture
Rotate which members are permitted to speak
Foster an inclusive environment that values diverse perspectives
items.explanation: Inclusive leadership leverages diversity for better outcomes. Forcing one style suppresses difference, favouring a majority culture is exclusionary, and rationing who may speak undermines psychological safety.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Team

items.stem: A project's deliverables are technically complete but will not create the intended benefit until users adopt them. What should the project manager do?
options: Focus on enabling adoption and benefits realization with the users
Declare the project complete because the deliverables are built
Hand the deliverables to operations and close the project
Start the next phase without addressing adoption
items.explanation: The aim of a project is to deliver business value, so adoption and benefits must be managed. Declaring completion on output alone or closing before adoption ignores value, and moving on leaves the benefits unrealized.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Process domain

items.stem: Stakeholders complain that project reports are too detailed and hard to act on. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Ask the sponsor to interpret the reports for stakeholders
Adapt the content and format of communication to stakeholder needs
Continue sending the same reports to avoid inconsistency
Stop reporting until stakeholders ask for updates
items.explanation: Communication must be tailored to audience needs to be effective. Persisting with unusable reports wastes effort, stopping reporting breaks transparency, and using the sponsor as a translator is inefficient.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Process domain

items.stem: A critical message must reach a dispersed team and the sender needs confirmation that it was understood. Which communication method is MOST appropriate?
options: A notice posted on a shared drive
A one-line chat message to the group
An interactive live session where understanding can be confirmed
A mass email with no acknowledgement requested
items.explanation: Interactive communication is best when confirmation of understanding is required. Email, posted notices, and chat are push methods that cannot reliably confirm comprehension, especially for a critical message.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Project Work

items.stem: During planning, a new risk is identified that could delay a key vendor shipment. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Ignore it until the shipment is actually late
Immediately notify the sponsor of a schedule failure
Remove the shipment from the schedule baseline
Record and analyze the risk, then plan an appropriate response
items.explanation: Risks are identified, analyzed, and planned for in the risk register. Waiting turns a risk into an issue, reporting a failure that has not occurred is premature, and altering the baseline is not a risk response.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Process domain

items.stem: A risk has high probability and high impact, and the team decides to purchase insurance to move the financial exposure to a third party. Which risk response is this?
options: Transfer
Avoid
Mitigate
Accept
items.explanation: Transfer shifts the impact and ownership to a third party, for example through insurance. Avoidance removes the risk entirely, mitigation reduces probability or impact, and acceptance retains the risk.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Risk Management

items.stem: A risk has a 30 percent chance of costing the project $40,000. What is the expected monetary value of this risk?
items.explanation: EMV equals probability times impact, so 0.30 times $40,000 = $12,000. The other figures incorrectly use the raw impact, the probability alone, or an unrelated amount.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Risk Management

items.stem: A vendor option carries a 25 percent chance of a $20,000 penalty and a 75 percent chance of no penalty. What is the expected monetary value of the penalty?
items.explanation: EMV equals 0.25 times $20,000 = $5,000. Listing the full penalty, the probability-weighted complement, or an unrelated amount does not reflect expected value.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Risk Management

items.stem: The team can eliminate a risk by redesigning the solution to remove the risky component entirely. Which risk response is this?
options: Mitigate
Transfer
Accept
Avoid
items.explanation: Avoidance removes the threat by changing the plan or scope. Mitigation only reduces it, transfer shifts it, and acceptance retains it without action.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Risk Management

items.stem: A low-probability, low-impact risk is documented with no active response, and reserves are set aside for it. Which response is this?
options: Accept
Exploit
Avoid
Enhance
items.explanation: Acceptance acknowledges a risk and sets aside a reserve rather than acting on it. Exploit and enhance are opportunity responses, and avoid is a threat-elimination response.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Risk Management

items.stem: The team can guarantee an early delivery by assigning the best engineer to a high-value task, deliberately capturing the opportunity. Which response is this?
options: Accept
Exploit
Enhance
Share
items.explanation: Exploit ensures an opportunity is realized by using the best resources or actions. Enhance increases the chance but does not guarantee it, share partners with a third party, and accept does not pursue the opportunity.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Risk Management

items.stem: A risk response has been agreed with the team. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Remove the risk from the register since it is resolved
Inform the sponsor but record nothing
Update the risk register with the response, owner, and actions
Wait until the risk occurs to act
items.explanation: Agreed responses are recorded in the risk register with an owner and actions so they can be tracked. Waiting defeats planning, removing the risk discards monitoring, and recording nothing loses traceability.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Risk Management

items.stem: A problem has already occurred and is affecting the project. How should the project manager handle it?
options: Treat it as a new risk and only analyze probability
Wait to see whether it resolves itself
Ignore it because it was not in the risk register
Log it and manage it as an issue with an owner and resolution actions
items.explanation: An event that has already happened is an issue, managed in the issue log with an owner and actions. Treating it as a future risk misclassifies it, and waiting or ignoring lets the impact grow.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Risk Management

items.stem: A new stakeholder with high influence appears late in the project. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Identify and analyze the stakeholder, then update the engagement approach
Continue with the existing stakeholder plan unchanged
Wait for the stakeholder to make contact
Ask the sponsor to manage the new stakeholder
items.explanation: A new high-influence stakeholder must be identified and analyzed so the engagement plan can adapt. Ignoring them is risky, waiting cedes initiative, and offloading to the sponsor abandons relationship management.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Process domain

items.stem: An influential stakeholder is currently resistant but has the power to block the project. Which engagement strategy is MOST appropriate?
options: Defer all engagement until delivery
Engage them closely to understand concerns and move them toward support
Monitor them with minimal communication
Provide only routine status reports
items.explanation: High-power, resistant stakeholders need active engagement to reduce risk of obstruction. Monitoring, routine reporting, or deferring interaction leaves a powerful detractor unaddressed.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Stakeholders

items.stem: A project has a cost performance index (CPI) of 0.8. What does this BEST indicate?
options: The project is under budget
The project is exactly on budget
The project has spent more than planned for the work completed
The project is ahead of schedule
items.explanation: CPI below 1.0 means cost inefficiency, so the project is over budget for the work performed. A CPI above 1.0 would indicate under budget, and CPI says nothing directly about the schedule.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Cost Management

items.stem: Planned value is $100,000 and earned value is $80,000. What does the schedule variance indicate?
options: A positive variance of $20,000, meaning the project is ahead of schedule
A $20,000 cost overrun
A zero variance, meaning the project is on schedule
A negative variance of $20,000, meaning the project is behind schedule
items.explanation: Schedule variance equals earned value minus planned value, so $80,000 minus $100,000 = -$20,000, indicating less work completed than planned. The other options misstate the sign, confuse cost and schedule, or deny the variance.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Cost Management

items.stem: The budget at completion is $200,000 and the cost performance index is 0.8. Using estimate at completion equal to budget at completion divided by CPI, what is the estimate at completion?
items.explanation: EAC equals BAC divided by CPI, so $200,000 / 0.8 = $250,000, forecasting a cost overrun if efficiency persists. The other figures multiply incorrectly or assume no variance.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Cost Management

items.stem: A team needs a quick order-of-magnitude estimate before detailed planning is available. Which estimating technique is MOST appropriate?
options: A full schedule simulation
Analogous estimating based on similar past projects
Bottom-up estimating of every work package
Detailed three-point estimating of each activity
items.explanation: Analogous estimating uses historical data for a fast, high-level figure when little detail exists. Bottom-up and three-point methods require detail and time, and simulation is unnecessary at this stage.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Schedule Management

items.stem: Using PERT, optimistic is 4 days, most likely is 8 days, and pessimistic is 18 days. What is the expected duration?
options: 8 days
12 days
9 days
10 days
items.explanation: PERT weightings give (4 + 4*8 + 18) / 6 = 54 / 6 = 9 days. The other values come from averaging incorrectly or ignoring the weighting.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Schedule Management

items.stem: What does the critical path of a project determine?
options: The activities with the largest budgets
The activities assigned to the most senior staff
The risks with the highest impact
The shortest possible project duration through the longest chain of dependent activities
items.explanation: The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent activities, which sets the shortest possible project duration. Budget, staffing, and risk are not properties that define the critical path.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Schedule Management

items.stem: How much total float does an activity on the critical path have?
options: Zero float
One day
The same float as the project buffer
Unlimited float
items.explanation: By definition, activities on the critical path have zero total float, so any delay moves the project end date. Non-critical activities may have positive float.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Schedule Management

items.stem: The project must finish sooner without changing scope, so the team adds resources to critical-path activities to shorten their durations. Which technique is this?
options: Re-baselining
Crashing
Fast tracking
Resource leveling
items.explanation: Crashing adds resources to shorten duration, usually at increased cost. Fast tracking overlaps activities, resource leveling resolves over-allocation, and re-baselining changes the approved baseline.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Schedule Management

items.stem: The team overlaps two normally sequential activities to shorten the schedule and accepts the rework risk. Which technique is this?
options: Resource smoothing
Rolling wave planning
Fast tracking
Crashing
items.explanation: Fast tracking performs sequential activities in parallel and trades schedule for rework risk. Crashing adds resources, smoothing adjusts resources within float, and rolling wave planning defers detail.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Schedule Management

items.stem: For what is the contingency reserve of a project BEST used?
options: Responding to unknown-unknowns outside the plan
Funding unapproved scope changes
Increasing the project's profit margin
Responding to identified risks if they occur
items.explanation: Contingency reserves cover identified risks, while management reserves address unknown-unknowns. Using contingency for scope changes or profit is not its purpose.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Cost Management

items.stem: The project must buy a specialized component and the requirements are clearly defined. Which contract type is BEST for the buyer?
options: Firm fixed-price
Cost plus percentage of cost
Time and materials
Cost reimbursable
items.explanation: A firm fixed-price contract places cost risk on the seller when requirements are well defined. Cost-reimbursable and time-and-materials types expose the buyer to cost growth, and cost plus percentage of cost gives the seller no incentive to control cost.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Procurement Management

items.stem: The scope of a purchased service is unclear and expected to evolve rapidly. Which contract type is MOST appropriate?
options: Lump-sum
Time and materials
Firm fixed-price
Fixed-price incentive fee
items.explanation: Time-and-materials contracts suit uncertain, evolving scope because work is paid as consumed. Fixed-price forms require a stable scope, and lump-sum is a fixed-price variant unsuited to change.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Procurement Management

items.stem: The team must decide whether to build a component internally or purchase it. Which analysis is MOST appropriate?
options: Reserve analysis
Root cause analysis
Make-or-buy analysis
Earned value analysis
items.explanation: Make-or-buy analysis weighs the cost and capability of internal versus external delivery. Earned value, reserve, and root cause analyses do not answer the build-or-buy question.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Procurement Management

items.stem: Before issuing a request for proposal, what must the project manager ensure the procurement document contains?
options: The names of the preferred vendor's staff
The project's internal cost baseline
A guarantee of award to the lowest bidder
A clear statement of work describing the required deliverables
items.explanation: A clear statement of work is essential so vendors bid on the same requirement. Including competitor staff names, internal cost data, or an award guarantee is inappropriate and can distort fair competition.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Procurement Management

items.stem: Several vendors respond to a request for proposal. What should the project manager do to select the best one?
options: Evaluate the proposals against agreed weighted criteria
Choose the vendor with the lowest price alone
Select the vendor the team already knows
Award to whichever vendor responds first
items.explanation: Weighted criteria make the selection objective and aligned to project needs. Lowest price ignores quality, familiarity is biased, and first-response selection has no basis.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Procurement Management

items.stem: The team inspects deliverables at the end of production to remove defects before delivery. Which quality concept does this represent?
options: A quality audit
Quality control
Quality assurance
Quality planning
items.explanation: Inspection to detect defects is quality control. Quality assurance focuses on improving processes, quality planning defines how standards will be met, and an audit reviews process compliance.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Quality Management

items.stem: The project manager wants to reduce the total cost of quality. Which action BEST aligns with this goal?
options: Add more rework capacity
Accept more defects as normal
Prevent defects earlier rather than fixing them later
Increase end-of-line inspection
items.explanation: Prevention costs less than correction, so investing earlier reduces the overall cost of quality. More inspection or rework capacity increases appraisal and failure costs, and accepting defects raises failure costs.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Quality Management

items.stem: A process is repeatedly producing defects. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Inspect and rework each defective item
Increase the number of inspectors
Add the defects to the issue log only
Analyze and improve the process that is creating the defects
items.explanation: Repeating defects signal a process problem, so quality assurance should improve the process root cause. Inspecting and reworking treats symptoms, more inspectors add cost, and logging alone does not fix the cause.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Quality Management

items.stem: A deliverable meets its specifications but the customer must formally accept it. Which activity handles this formal acceptance?
options: Validate scope
Control quality
Control scope
Plan quality
items.explanation: Validate scope is where the customer formally accepts completed deliverables. Control quality verifies correctness internally, control scope manages scope changes, and plan quality defines standards.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Scope Management

items.stem: A stakeholder requests a new feature in the middle of the project. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Ask the team to work overtime to absorb it
Assess the request's impact through the change control process
Add the feature immediately to keep the stakeholder happy
Reject the request outright
items.explanation: Every change should be evaluated for impact before decisions are made. Accepting immediately causes scope creep, blanket rejection ignores value, and overtime compensates without authority.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Integration Management

items.stem: Small extra requests are being added without approval, and the scope is growing steadily. What should the project manager do?
options: Reduce quality to keep the schedule unchanged
Stop communicating with the requesting stakeholder
Enforce change control and assess the impact of each request
Continue absorbing the small requests to avoid conflict
items.explanation: Uncontrolled additions are scope creep, so change control must be applied. Absorbing them erodes the baseline, cutting quality is a poor trade-off, and ceasing communication damages the relationship.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Scope Management

items.stem: The team cannot estimate the work because it is defined too broadly at the top level. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Estimate the whole project as a single number
Skip estimating until delivery begins
Ask the sponsor to estimate the work
Decompose the work into smaller, manageable components
items.explanation: Decomposition into a work breakdown structure produces components small enough to estimate and manage. Estimating the whole as one number is unreliable, skipping estimation risks control, and the sponsor is not the estimator.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Scope Management

items.stem: What does the scope baseline consist of?
options: The scope statement, the work breakdown structure, and the WBS dictionary
The schedule baseline and cost baseline
The risk register and issue log
The communications and stakeholder plans
items.explanation: The scope baseline is the approved scope statement, WBS, and WBS dictionary. Schedule, cost, risk, and stakeholder documents are separate baselines and plans, not components of the scope baseline.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Scope Management

items.stem: Different stakeholder groups submit conflicting requirements. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Escalate the conflict to the sponsor immediately
Facilitate requirements analysis and prioritization with the stakeholders
Select the requirements from the most senior group
Document all requirements and implement them all
items.explanation: Facilitating analysis and prioritization resolves conflicts against project objectives. Deferring to seniority ignores merit, implementing everything may be infeasible, and immediate escalation bypasses a resolvable step.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Process domain

items.stem: Several subsidiary plans are complete, but the project still lacks a coordinated plan. What should the project manager do?
options: Use only the schedule and ignore the other plans
Ask the PMO to write the project management plan
Consolidate the subsidiary plans into an integrated project management plan
Keep each plan separate and manage them independently
items.explanation: Integration means consolidating the subsidiary plans into one coordinated project management plan. Managing plans in isolation creates conflicts, ignoring them loses control, and delegating to the PMO avoids the project manager's role.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Integration Management

items.stem: A project is about to start execution. What should be approved before work formally begins?
options: The final lessons learned report
The closure documents
The procurement audit report
The project management plan and its baselines
items.explanation: Execution begins after the project management plan and baselines are approved, giving authority to proceed. Lessons learned, closure, and procurement audit outputs occur later in the project life cycle.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Integration Management

items.stem: An approved change has just been implemented. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Update the affected baselines and plans and communicate the change
Return to the change control board for a second approval
Close the project change log
Undo the change if it affects the schedule
items.explanation: Implementing a change means updating affected plans and baselines and informing stakeholders. Re-approving is unnecessary, closing the log loses history, and undoing an approved change is incorrect.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Integration Management

items.stem: A proposed change has major cost and schedule impact. Who should approve it?
options: Any single stakeholder who benefits from it
The change control board or the authority defined in the change management plan
The project manager alone
The team member who proposed it
items.explanation: Large changes require approval at the level defined by governance, typically the change control board. The project manager alone, the proposer, or one beneficiary cannot approve major baseline impacts.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Integration Management

items.stem: A project is closing and the project manager wants to capture value for future work. What is the BEST action?
options: Keep lessons learned only within the team
Wait until a future project asks for them
Document lessons learned and add them to the organizational knowledge base
Discard project records to save storage
items.explanation: Lessons learned become organizational process assets that improve future projects when documented and shared. Discarding or hoarding them loses value, and waiting means the insight may be lost.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Project Work

items.stem: A project is cancelled before completion. What should the project manager do?
options: Stop all work immediately and leave records incomplete
Continue spending the remaining budget
Refuse to close until the full scope is delivered
Perform closure activities, document lessons learned, and release resources
items.explanation: Even a cancelled project still requires closure, documentation, and resource release. Abandoning records, continuing spend, or refusing to close ignores the project manager's closure responsibilities.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Integration Management

items.stem: A deliverable is ready and the operations team will support it after go-live. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Plan the transition and handover to operations
Close the project without involving operations
Leave operations to discover the system on their own
Delay handover until operations request it
items.explanation: A planned transition to operations ensures continuity and adoption. Closing without handover or leaving operations unsupported risks failure, and passive delay puts the service at risk.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Process domain

items.stem: The project manager will leave the project midway. What is MOST important before they go?
options: Announce the departure with no handover
Ensure knowledge transfer and current documentation for the successor
Take project records with them for their own reference
Complete any individual tasks they personally own and leave
items.explanation: Knowledge transfer and up-to-date documentation protect continuity. Taking records or leaving without a handover introduces risk, and the project continues beyond any single person's tasks.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Process domain

items.stem: Requirements are stable and heavy documentation is required for regulatory compliance. Which delivery approach is MOST appropriate?
options: An approach that skips formal reviews
A no-planning approach based on improvisation
A predictive plan-driven approach
A purely agile approach with no documentation
items.explanation: Stable requirements and documentation needs favour a predictive approach. A pure agile or no-documentation approach conflicts with compliance, and skipping reviews or planning undermines control.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Development Approach and Life Cycle

items.stem: A project has a fixed regulatory deadline but the requirements will keep evolving. Which approach is BEST?
options: A purely predictive approach with a frozen scope
A purely agile approach with no governance
An approach with no milestone commitments
A hybrid approach combining predictive governance with agile delivery
items.explanation: Hybrid approaches pair the predictability needed for a hard deadline with the flexibility to absorb evolving requirements. A frozen scope ignores change, and dropping governance ignores the deadline commitment.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Development Approach and Life Cycle

items.stem: The customer wants frequent feedback and early delivery of value. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: An iterative and incremental agile approach
A single big-bang delivery at the end
An approach that delivers only documentation early
An approach that avoids customer involvement until launch
items.explanation: Agile iterative delivery gives early value and frequent feedback. Big-bang delivery defers feedback, documentation is not value, and excluding the customer contradicts the goal.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: An agile team estimates work using story points. What do story points primarily measure?
options: The number of defects expected
Relative size or effort of work, not elapsed time
The exact number of hours the work will take
The cost of each story in currency
items.explanation: Story points express relative size or effort and should not be equated to hours. Converting them to exact time, cost, or expected defects misuses the technique.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: Mid-iteration the product owner wants to reprioritize the backlog to add new work. What should the project manager do?
options: Cancel the iteration and start over
Ignore the product owner until the project ends
Protect the current iteration and reprioritize for the next one unless the change is critical
Immediately swap new work into the active iteration
items.explanation: Iterations are protected from churn so the team can meet their commitment, with reprioritization applied at iteration boundaries unless critical. Swapping work or cancelling disrupts the sprint, and ignoring the product owner rejects their role.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: What is the primary purpose of the daily stand-up?
options: To report detailed status to the project manager
To assign new tasks to each member
To update the project schedule baseline
To synchronize the team and surface impediments
items.explanation: The stand-up synchronizes the team and raises blockers. It is not a status report to the project manager, a task-assignment meeting, or where the baseline is updated.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: How is planning handled in agile delivery?
options: Continuously, at the start of each iteration and as needed
Only once at the very beginning of the project
Only during project closure
Only when the customer demands it
items.explanation: Agile planning is continuous, re-examined each iteration using progressive elaboration. Planning only at the start, at closure, or on demand does not support adapting to change.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: Who should attend the sprint review?
options: No one outside the team
The team and key stakeholders, who inspect the increment and adapt the backlog
Only the developers
Only the project manager and sponsor
