items.explanation: The sprint review is where the team and stakeholders inspect the increment and adapt the backlog. Limiting it to developers or leaders, or excluding stakeholders, removes the feedback the event exists to produce.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: What is the main focus of a retrospective?
options: Estimating the next release in detail
Reporting status to the sponsor
Inspecting the way the team works and identifying improvements
Reviewing the product increment with customers
items.explanation: A retrospective inspects the process and team interactions to improve how work is done. Product inspection happens in the review, estimation belongs to planning, and status reporting is separate.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: Decision rights and escalation paths for the project are unclear. What should the project manager do?
options: Make all decisions personally to fill the gap
Let the team escalate to the sponsor directly each time
Wait for the PMO to notice the gap
Establish or clarify a project governance structure and plan
items.explanation: Clear governance defines who decides and how issues escalate. Centralizing every decision defeats governance, ad hoc escalation is inconsistent, and waiting leaves the gap unresolved.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Process domain

items.stem: The project must pass phase gates to continue. What should the project manager do before each gate?
options: Verify that exit criteria are met and prepare the required review evidence
Skip the gate if the team is confident
Proceed to the next phase and backfill evidence later
Ask the sponsor to waive the gate every time
items.explanation: Phase gates confirm that exit criteria are satisfied before proceeding. Skipping, backfilling, or routinely waiving gates defeats the governance they provide.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Project Work

items.stem: An issue has been assigned to a team member to resolve. What should the project manager do to keep it on track?
options: Move it into the risk register
Record it in the issue log with an owner and follow up until it is closed
Rely on the team member to report back on their own
Forget it now that the team member owns it
items.explanation: Issues are tracked in the issue log with owners and status until resolved. Relying on informal reporting, forgetting it, or reclassifying an occurred issue as a risk loses control.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Risk Management

items.stem: An issue cannot be resolved at the team level. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Inform external parties without authority
Close the issue to clear the log
Escalate per the governance plan with a clear impact analysis
Keep the issue internal indefinitely
items.explanation: When an issue exceeds the team's ability to resolve it, escalate through governance with supporting impact information. Keeping it internal or closing it hides the problem, and uncoordinated external communication is inappropriate.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Process domain

items.stem: When the project manager prioritizes work, what should be the PRIMARY consideration?
options: Whichever task is easiest to start
The personal preference of the team
The task that was requested most recently
The business value and benefits the work delivers
items.explanation: Prioritization should follow business value and alignment to objectives. Ease, personal preference, or recency are not value-based criteria and can misdirect effort.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Process domain

items.stem: The team is spending significant time on low-value work while high-value items wait. What should the project manager do?
options: Refocus the team on the highest-value prioritized items
Let the team continue for the sake of consistency
Add more low-value tasks to fill capacity
Increase the team size to cover everything
items.explanation: Effort should follow value, so the work must be reprioritized. Continuing misaligned work wastes capacity, adding more low-value work compounds the problem, and simply growing the team may not address prioritization.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: A deliverable is complete but stakeholders report they see no benefit. What should the project manager do?
options: Wait for the benefit to appear on its own
Assess benefits realization and adoption, and address the gap with stakeholders
Insist that the benefit exists because the deliverable is done
Close the project since the deliverable is complete
items.explanation: Benefits must be realized, not assumed, so the gap between output and outcome should be examined. Denying the feedback, closing prematurely, or passively waiting fails to deliver the intended value.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Process domain

items.stem: The team disagrees about when a user story is truly finished. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the customer to inspect every small task
Declare a story done once code is written
Agree on a clear definition of done and acceptance criteria with the team
Let each member decide for their own work
items.explanation: A shared definition of done and acceptance criteria remove ambiguity. Individual definitions create inconsistency, customer inspection at task level is excessive, and code-complete is rarely an adequate definition of done.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: The project manager wants to measure quality objectively. What should they do?
options: Rely on the team's general impression of quality
Wait until customers complain
Measure only the final cost of the project
Define quality metrics and measure performance against them
items.explanation: Quality is managed with defined metrics and measurement. Impressions are subjective, waiting for complaints is reactive, and cost alone does not measure quality.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Quality Management

items.stem: A team of 10 people needs to know how many communication channels exist. Using n(n-1)/2, what is the number of channels?
items.explanation: The formula n(n-1)/2 gives 10 times 9 divided by 2 = 45 channels, illustrating why communication complexity grows quickly with team size. The other figures use the wrong arithmetic.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Communications Management

items.stem: A critical resource is over-allocated across activities. Which technique adjusts the schedule to resolve the over-allocation, possibly extending duration?
options: Fast tracking
Resource leveling
Resource smoothing
Crashing
items.explanation: Resource leveling resolves over-allocation and can change the critical path or extend the schedule. Resource smoothing uses float without extending the schedule, and crashing or fast tracking compress rather than level resources.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Resource Management

items.stem: A key milestone slips by a week. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Blame the responsible team member in the status report
Cancel the milestone from the baseline
Assess the impact, update the schedule, and communicate with stakeholders
Silently move the milestone without telling anyone
items.explanation: Impact assessment, schedule updates, and transparent communication are the correct response to slippage. Silent changes, blame, or removing the milestone destroy trust and control.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Schedule Management

items.stem: Project costs are exceeding the approved budget. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Reduce quality to recover the budget
Request additional funds without analysis
Wait until the next reporting cycle to act
Analyze the cost variance and take corrective action
items.explanation: Cost variances are analyzed and corrected promptly. Cutting quality harms the deliverable, requesting funds without analysis is unjustified, and waiting lets the variance grow.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Cost Management

items.stem: What is the difference between contingency reserve and management reserve?
options: Contingency reserve is for identified risks; management reserve is for unknown-unknowns
Contingency reserve is for unknown-unknowns; management reserve is for known risks
Both reserves are the same and used interchangeably
Neither reserve is part of the project budget
items.explanation: Contingency reserve covers identified risks within the cost baseline, while management reserve covers unknown-unknowns and sits above the baseline. The options that swap or merge the two, or exclude them from the budget, are incorrect.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Cost Management

items.stem: A project has a schedule performance index (SPI) of 0.9. What does this indicate?
options: The project is on schedule
The project is behind schedule
The project is ahead of schedule
The project is over budget
items.explanation: SPI below 1.0 means less work has been completed than planned, so the project is behind schedule. SPI above 1.0 is ahead, and cost status is indicated by CPI, not SPI.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Schedule Management

items.stem: Most of the project's defects come from a small number of causes. Which tool BEST helps prioritize where to act?
options: A resource histogram
A stakeholder grid
A Pareto chart
A control chart
items.explanation: A Pareto chart ranks causes by frequency, highlighting the vital few. A control chart tracks process stability, a resource histogram shows allocation, and a stakeholder grid maps influence and interest.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Quality Management

items.stem: The team needs to identify the root causes of a recurring problem. Which tool is MOST appropriate?
options: A Gantt chart
An earned value report
A RACI chart
A cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram
items.explanation: A cause-and-effect diagram organizes possible root causes for analysis. A Gantt chart shows schedule, an earned value report shows performance, and a RACI chart shows responsibilities.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Quality Management

items.stem: A process has been running within its control limits for some time. What should the project manager do?
options: Avoid unnecessary tampering and investigate only special-cause variation
Adjust the process continuously to improve it
Stop the process until variation is zero
Ignore the control chart going forward
items.explanation: A stable process should not be tampered with, because reacting to common-cause variation worsens outcomes; investigate only special causes. Continuous adjustment, stopping the process, or ignoring the chart are all inappropriate.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Quality Management

items.stem: The project manager wants to confirm that project processes comply with the organization's standards. What should be done?
options: Add more contingency reserve
Conduct a quality audit
Perform end-of-line inspection
Rework the deliverables
items.explanation: A quality audit verifies process compliance with standards and identifies improvements. Inspection checks the product, rework fixes defects, and adding reserve is unrelated to compliance.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Quality Management

items.stem: A deliverable has been verified as correct internally. What must happen next for formal closure?
options: Add it to the risk register
Update the resource histogram
Obtain formal acceptance of the deliverable from the customer
Rework it again to be safe
items.explanation: Verified deliverables must be formally accepted by the customer through validate scope. Unnecessary rework adds cost, and the risk register or resource histogram are not part of acceptance.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Scope Management

items.stem: The team is unclear about who is accountable for each project task. Which tool BEST addresses this?
options: A Pareto chart
A control chart
A burn-down chart
A responsibility assignment matrix such as RACI
items.explanation: A RACI or responsibility assignment matrix clarifies who is responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed. Pareto and control charts address quality, and a burn-down chart tracks remaining work.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Resource Management

items.stem: Where does the project manager record stakeholder information and current engagement levels?
options: The stakeholder register
The risk register
The issue log
The work breakdown structure
items.explanation: Stakeholder identification and engagement levels are recorded in the stakeholder register. The risk register tracks risks, the issue log tracks issues, and the WBS decomposes scope.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Stakeholders

items.stem: A previously supportive stakeholder has become resistant. What should the project manager do?
options: Report the stakeholder as a risk owner
Reassess the stakeholder's engagement and adapt the approach
Continue with the original engagement plan unchanged
Remove the stakeholder from communications
items.explanation: Engagement levels change, so the project manager should reassess and adapt. Sticking to an outdated plan, cutting communication, or mislabeling the person ignores the relationship problem.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Stakeholders

items.stem: Meetings frequently end without clear outcomes or follow-up. What should the project manager do?
options: Stop holding meetings and rely on email
Let participants decide outcomes afterward
Set clear agendas and capture decisions and action items with owners
Hold longer meetings to cover more ground
items.explanation: Agendas plus captured decisions and owned actions make meetings productive. Longer meetings add fatigue, abandoning meetings loses collaboration, and leaving outcomes undefined repeats the problem.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 7th edition - Project Work

items.stem: The team can deliver a minimal but genuinely usable increment early. What should the project manager do?
options: Hold all delivery until the full scope is complete
Deliver the increment without stakeholder feedback
Wait for the next budget cycle to release it
Deliver the usable increment early to realize value sooner
items.explanation: Delivering usable increments early is the fastest path to value and feedback. Withholding until full scope delays benefit, skipping feedback misses learning, and an artificial delay adds no value.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: The customer rejects a submitted deliverable. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Understand the gap between the deliverable and the acceptance criteria
Argue that the deliverable meets the specification
Resubmit the same deliverable unchanged
Escalate the rejection to the sponsor immediately
items.explanation: The first step is to understand why acceptance failed against the criteria so the gap can be closed. Arguing or resubmitting wastes time, and immediate escalation bypasses a resolvable quality issue.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Scope Management

items.stem: A high-priority risk response has been planned but has no one responsible for it. What should the project manager do?
options: Downgrade its priority so it needs no owner
Assign a risk owner to carry out and monitor the response
Leave it unassigned and hope the team acts
Remove the risk from the register
items.explanation: Every planned response needs a risk owner accountable for it. Leaving it unassigned means it likely will not be executed, and removing or downgrading a high-priority risk neglects real exposure.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Risk Management

items.stem: A vendor contract has been completed to the buyer's satisfaction. What should the project manager do?
options: Withhold final documentation from the vendor
Renew the contract automatically without review
Formally close the procurement and document the vendor's performance
Leave the contract open in case of future needs
items.explanation: Completed procurements are formally closed and seller performance is recorded for future selection. Leaving the contract open, withholding documentation, or auto-renewing without review are all incorrect.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Procurement Management

items.stem: The schedule plan and the cost plan conflict with each other. What should the project manager do?
options: Follow the schedule plan and ignore the cost plan
Follow the cost plan and ignore the schedule plan
Baseline both as they are and resolve conflicts during execution
Reconcile them through integrated planning and trade-off analysis
items.explanation: Integration reconciles competing plans through trade-off analysis before baselining. Ignoring one plan loses control, and baselining unresolved conflicts guarantees disruption later.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Integration Management

items.stem: The project depends on an assumption that may prove false. What should the project manager do?
options: Validate the assumption and record it in the assumption log
Treat it as a guaranteed fact
Forget it because assumptions are always safe
Convert it into a hard constraint
items.explanation: Assumptions carry risk, so they should be validated and logged. Treating them as facts or constraints without validation is dangerous, and ignoring them removes the chance to react if they fail.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Risk Management

items.stem: A regulatory deadline fixes the project's end date and cannot move. How should the project manager plan?
options: Promise all scope will be delivered regardless
Plan within the fixed constraint and prioritize or adjust scope accordingly
Plan an end date beyond the deadline anyway
Ignore the deadline until late in the project
items.explanation: When time is a hard constraint, scope or resources must be adjusted and work prioritized to the deadline. Planning past the deadline, ignoring it, or overpromising scope sets the project up to fail.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Schedule Management

items.stem: The sponsor wants faster delivery and lower cost with the same scope. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Reduce quality to satisfy speed and cost
Refuse to discuss the request
Analyze the trade-offs and present the sponsor with the realistic options
Accept all three constraints and push the team harder
items.explanation: The triple constraint requires trade-offs, so the project manager should analyze and present options. Accepting all three, cutting quality, or refusing to engage ignores the mathematical reality of the constraints.
items.reference: PMBOK Guide 6th edition - Project Integration Management

items.stem: Two stakeholder groups hold conflicting priorities for the next increment. What should the project manager do?
options: Prioritize the group that speaks first
Build both groups' priorities regardless of capacity
Defer all work until the groups agree on their own
Facilitate prioritization against the project objectives and value
items.explanation: Facilitated prioritization against objectives resolves conflicting demands. First-come, building everything, or indefinite deferral all fail to prioritize by value and capacity.
items.reference: Agile Practice Guide (PMI)

items.stem: After delivery, users are struggling to adopt the solution. What should the project manager do?
options: Provide transition support such as training and track benefits realization
Declare the project successful and withdraw all support
Blame the users for not reading the documentation
Revert to the previous solution without analysis
items.explanation: Adoption is part of realizing value, so transition support and benefits tracking are needed. Withdrawing support, blaming users, or reverting without analysis fails the intended outcome.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Process domain

items.stem: The team is ready to start a new phase, but lessons from the previous phase have not been reviewed. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Only capture lessons if the phase failed
Review lessons learned from the previous phase to improve the next one
Begin the new phase and review lessons at project closure only
Discard the lessons because the phase is finished
items.explanation: Knowledge transfer between phases, not just at closure, improves each subsequent phase. Deferring, discarding, or capturing lessons only after failure misses the chance to apply them.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Process domain

items.stem: A new data privacy regulation will affect the project's solution. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Assume the legal department will handle it without input
Remove the affected features to avoid the regulation
Assess the regulation's impact and ensure the project complies
Continue as planned and address compliance after go-live
items.explanation: Compliance is a Business Environment responsibility, so the impact must be assessed and built into the plan. Deferring, ignoring it, or cutting features without analysis all create legal and delivery risk.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Business Environment domain

items.stem: The project must comply with industry regulations. What should the project manager do to ensure compliance?
options: Wait for an audit to find any compliance gaps
Assume the team already knows the regulations
Document compliance only if a problem arises
Identify the compliance requirements and build controls into the project plan
items.explanation: Compliance requirements should be identified early and controlled through the plan. Waiting for an audit, assuming knowledge, or documenting only after a problem are reactive and risky.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Business Environment domain

items.stem: A regulation changes midway through the project. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Assess the change's impact and manage it through change control and compliance review
Ignore it until the current phase is complete
Immediately halt the entire project
Inform the team to keep working as if nothing changed
items.explanation: A regulatory change is assessed for impact and managed through the change control process. Ignoring it risks non-compliance, halting the whole project is disproportionate, and pretending nothing changed is unsafe.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Business Environment domain

items.stem: How should the project manager evaluate whether the project delivered business value?
options: Check that every task in the schedule was completed
Measure benefits against the objectives in the business case
Count the number of deliverables produced
Confirm the budget was fully spent
items.explanation: Business value is judged by realized benefits against the business case, not by output volume or spend. Deliverables, budget usage, and task completion are means to an outcome, not evidence of value.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Business Environment domain

items.stem: The assumptions in the approved business case are no longer valid. What should the project manager do?
options: Cancel the project without consulting anyone
Hide the change from the sponsor to protect the project
Re-evaluate the business case with the sponsor and adjust direction as needed
Continue delivering against the outdated case
items.explanation: If the business case no longer holds, it must be revisited with the sponsor so the project stays aligned to value. Continuing an invalid case, cancelling unilaterally, or hiding the change are all unacceptable.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Business Environment domain

items.stem: A feature in scope no longer delivers business value. What should the project manager do?
options: Deliver it anyway because it is in scope
Delete it silently from the plan
Deliver it and add unnecessary cost to justify it
Review it with stakeholders and consider descoping it through change control
items.explanation: Value should drive scope, so a now-worthless feature is reviewed with stakeholders and removed through change control. Delivering it wastes resources, silently deleting it breaks governance, and inflating cost is dishonest.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Business Environment domain

items.stem: When should a project's benefits typically be measured?
options: After delivery, during operations, guided by the benefits realization plan
Only while the project is still executing
At the very first project meeting
Never, because benefits are impossible to measure
items.explanation: Benefits usually appear after the deliverable is in use, so they are tracked in operations against a benefits realization plan. Measuring only during execution or not at all fails to confirm value.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Business Environment domain

items.stem: A competitor releases a product that changes market conditions for the project. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Reduce the project's quality to compete on price
Assess the impact on project objectives with stakeholders and the sponsor
Ignore the competitor because it is outside the project
Immediately stop all project work
items.explanation: External business environment changes may affect scope and value, so their impact should be assessed with stakeholders. Ignoring, stopping work outright, or cutting quality without analysis are not reasoned responses.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Business Environment domain

items.stem: Economic conditions have raised the cost of key materials. What should the project manager do?
options: Hide the increase from the sponsor
Cut all contingency reserves immediately
Assess the impact on the budget and adjust forecasts and plans
Keep the original budget unchanged and hope costs fall
items.explanation: External cost changes are assessed and reflected in forecasts and plans. Leaving the budget static, concealing the change, or stripping reserves without analysis all impair control.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Business Environment domain

items.stem: A supplier is not meeting the compliance standards the project requires. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Accept the non-compliant work to keep the schedule
Terminate the supplier immediately without discussion
Ignore it because the supplier is external
Address the non-compliance with the supplier per the contract and compliance requirements
items.explanation: Non-compliance is addressed through the contract and compliance process. Accepting non-compliant work creates legal risk, immediate termination may be disproportionate, and ignoring an external supplier's non-compliance is unsafe.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Business Environment domain

items.stem: Users are resisting a new system because it changes their workflow. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Engage users to understand concerns and support adoption of the change
Force the change through without further discussion
Abandon the system and revert to the old process
Wait for users to adapt without any support
items.explanation: Organizational change succeeds when people are engaged and supported through the transition. Forcing it, abandoning the change, or passively waiting all undermine adoption and value.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Business Environment domain

items.stem: To increase the chance of adoption, what should the project manager do throughout the project?
options: Limit communication to reduce the risk of pushback
Apply change management practices such as communication, training, and stakeholder involvement
Address readiness only at go-live
Assume the sponsor will drive all adoption single-handedly
items.explanation: Change management is continuous, using communication, training, and involvement to build readiness. Waiting for go-live, relying on one person, or reducing communication all increase resistance.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Business Environment domain

items.stem: The project manager must choose between two initiatives with limited resources. What criterion should guide the choice?
options: The personal preference of the project team
Which initiative the project manager has done before
Alignment with and contribution to organizational business value
Which initiative is easier to start
items.explanation: Initiatives are prioritized by their contribution to business value and strategy. Ease, team preference, or prior experience are not valid value-based criteria for selection.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Business Environment domain

items.stem: The project generates records that regulators may inspect. What should the project manager ensure?
options: Records are deleted once the project closes
Records are kept only in a team member's personal files
Records are generated only when a regulator asks
Records are properly documented, retained, and accessible for compliance review
items.explanation: Compliance requires that required records be documented, retained, and retrievable. Deleting them, keeping them only personally, or creating them on demand violates retention and audit requirements.
items.reference: PMI PMP Exam Content Outline 2021 - Business Environment domain
